promptText: How does Context Engineering differ from Prompt Engineering?
options: Prompt Engineering is about how a single instruction is worded; Context Engineering decides, for every model call, the full set of information the model sees -- history, retrieved documents, tool outputs, memory, and the instructions -- including order and what is deliberately excluded
They are the same discipline under two different marketing names with no meaningful distinction
Context Engineering only applies to open-source models, while Prompt Engineering only applies to hosted APIs
Prompt Engineering handles retrieval, while Context Engineering handles wording and tone
explanation: A beautifully worded prompt sitting inside a badly assembled context window still fails, because the model cannot distinguish a carefully written instruction from noise that happened to arrive in the same request.

promptText: Is Context Engineering just another name for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
options: No -- RAG is one technique for populating a single zone of context (retrieved documents); Context Engineering is the broader discipline deciding how that output combines with history, tool results, memory, and instructions
Yes -- both terms describe the exact same pipeline with no meaningful difference
No -- RAG is a superset of Context Engineering that also includes model fine-tuning
Yes -- Context Engineering was renamed to RAG once vector databases became standard
explanation: A system can do sophisticated context engineering with no retrieval step at all, and a system can do RAG badly even with excellent retrieval if the surrounding assembly is careless -- RAG is a supplier to the pipeline, not the pipeline itself.

promptText: Why can't a production chat system simply include the full conversation history in every request?
options: The context window is finite, cost and latency rise with every included token, and models use information placed in the middle of a long context less reliably, so a bloated history can hurt quality even before hitting the hard token limit
Chat APIs technically reject any request containing more than one prior turn of history
Including history is a violation of most providers' terms of service
The model automatically discards conversation history after every third turn regardless of relevance
explanation: An ever-growing history eventually crowds out the budget for the current message and instructions, and quality can degrade well before the token limit is technically reached due to dilution and positional effects.

promptText: What is a 'context template' (or context schema), and how does it differ from a plain prompt string?
options: A context template defines named slots (instructions, examples, retrieved knowledge, history, current message) and rules for filling and ordering each one, producing a consistent, inspectable structure; a plain prompt string is just the final flattened output of that process
A context template is a compressed binary format that replaces plain-text prompts entirely to save tokens
A context template is only used for classification tasks and never applies to open-ended generation
A context template and a plain prompt string are identical; the term 'template' just refers to using triple-quoted strings in code
explanation: Treating the flattened string itself as the source of truth (editing it directly per call) is what leads to inconsistent, hard-to-audit prompts across a codebase -- the template with named slots is what stays maintainable.

promptText: What is the difference between a 'knowledge base' and 'context' in this discipline's vocabulary?
options: A knowledge base is a durable store of information existing independent of any particular model call (a document repository, a database, a vector index); context is the specific, transient slice of information actually assembled and sent to the model for one particular call
A knowledge base and context are interchangeable terms for the same underlying vector store
Context is always larger than the knowledge base it is derived from
A knowledge base only exists for RAG systems, while context only exists for fine-tuned models
explanation: Context Engineering is precisely the discipline of deciding how much of, and which parts of, a potentially enormous knowledge base become part of the necessarily small context for a given request.

promptText: What is 'context provenance,' and why does it matter for debugging?
options: Metadata attached to each piece of injected context recording where it came from (which document, tool call, or turn) -- without it, you cannot tell whether a wrong answer was a hallucination, a misread real source, or an outdated source
A cryptographic signature that prevents any context from being modified once assembled
A ranking algorithm that determines which model should process a given request
The practice of storing conversation history exclusively in a relational database instead of a vector store
explanation: With provenance you can trace an output back to the exact context that produced it, and it also lets the assistant cite sources to end users, materially increasing trust in the answer.

promptText: What is the practical implication of the 'lost in the middle' finding for how you assemble a prompt?
options: The most decision-critical instructions and the single most relevant retrieved fact should be placed near the start or end of the context, not left wherever they happened to land after concatenation, since models use middle-positioned information less reliably
Content in the middle of the context is processed twice by the attention mechanism, so it should be reserved for the least important material by design
The finding only applies to models under 1 billion parameters and is irrelevant to modern production systems
The fix is to always sort context alphabetically by source name so placement is deterministic
explanation: Models are measurably better at using information positioned near the beginning or end of context than information buried in the middle, even when relevance is identical -- so placement is a real design decision, not an afterthought.

promptText: A team raises a RAG pipeline's top-k retrieval count whenever an answer is wrong. Why is this often the wrong fix?
options: Every additional retrieved chunk competes for the model's limited attention; diluting relevant chunks with marginally relevant 'distractor' chunks can degrade answer quality even though more correct information is technically present -- a tighter relevance threshold or better re-ranking usually helps more
Raising top-k is never wrong because retrieval quality only ever improves as more documents are added, with no downside
Top-k only affects latency, never answer quality, so raising it is a purely safe operation
Higher top-k values are rejected outright by vector databases past a hardcoded limit of 3
explanation: This is the distractor-dilution problem: more retrieved context is not strictly safer context, since low-relevance chunks compete for the same limited attention as the chunk that actually mattered.

promptText: How does provider-side prompt-prefix caching change how you should order an assembled context?
options: Place parts of the context that are identical across many requests (system instructions, tool schemas, few-shot examples) at the very start, and parts that change every call (retrieved content, current message) at the end, since even a one-token change near the front invalidates the cached prefix for everything after it
Prefix caching means ordering no longer matters at all, since the entire prompt is cached regardless of structure
Prefix caching requires putting the current user message first so it can be cached before retrieval even runs
Prefix caching only applies to system prompts under 50 tokens, so ordering is irrelevant for larger prompts
explanation: This is an architectural design decision: keeping stable content in a consistent position and isolating volatile parts lets the stable prefix be reused instead of reprocessed on every call.

promptText: Why should a raw tool output (e.g., a 50-field JSON API response) typically NOT be pasted verbatim into the model's context?
options: Raw output is written for machines, not for a language model reading it as text -- large or noisy payloads should be normalized, labeled with provenance, and pruned to the fields the task actually needs before injection
Tool outputs are automatically rejected by the model's tokenizer if they contain JSON syntax
Verbatim tool output causes the model to switch into a special non-generative parsing mode that disables reasoning
Pasting tool output verbatim is fine and has no measurable effect on context budget or answer quality
explanation: A 50-line JSON response is usually reduced to the two or three fields the task needs, both to save budget and to avoid burying the relevant fields among irrelevant ones -- unpruned tool output is exactly the 'context rot' failure mode in long agentic loops.

promptText: When should retrieved or tool-derived context be injected as structured data (e.g., JSON) rather than natural-language prose?
options: When the downstream task needs precise, unambiguous fields like pricing, dates, IDs, or statuses, since prose paraphrasing risks the model silently altering a number or unit while 'helpfully' rewording it
Structured data should always be used for every context zone, since prose is strictly inferior in every scenario
Prose should always be used for every context zone, since structured data cannot be processed by attention mechanisms
The choice between structured and prose injection has no measurable effect on output accuracy
explanation: Prose works better for content meant to be read holistically and synthesized (a policy paragraph, a free-text ticket description); many production pipelines use both, matched to what each piece of content is for.

promptText: How does deliberate context engineering reduce hallucination in a way that is distinct from model-level techniques like fine-tuning?
options: A large share of production hallucination is the model being asked a question its assembled context didn't actually contain the answer to and answering anyway -- better retrieval, less dilution, and explicit absence-detection instructions fix this at the assembly layer, which is cheaper and faster than retraining
Context engineering reduces hallucination by lowering the model's temperature to 0 automatically on every call
Context engineering has no effect on hallucination; only fine-tuning can address it
Context engineering eliminates hallucination completely by guaranteeing the model always has perfect information
explanation: This is usually the first thing to fix before concluding a hallucination problem requires a model change -- ensuring the right facts are present and absence is detectable addresses the root cause in many production cases.

promptText: A RAG-based assistant gives a wrong answer even though the correct document was successfully retrieved by the vector search step. Using a context-engineering lens, what should you check first, and why is checking retrieval results in isolation insufficient?
options: Inspect the actual assembled context sent for that specific call -- retrieval succeeding doesn't guarantee the chunk survived assembly; it may have been crowded out by low-value chunks, landed in a 'lost in the middle' position, been truncated by a naive end-of-string budget cut, or been discarded during history summarization
Retrieval results and assembled context are always identical, so checking retrieval logs alone is sufficient to diagnose any RAG failure
The only possible cause is that the embedding model is outdated and needs to be replaced immediately
This class of failure can only be fixed by switching to a larger foundation model, since assembly has no bearing on answer quality once the correct document is retrieved
explanation: Without instrumentation that logs or reconstructs the exact final context per call, this class of bug is nearly undebuggable, because several independent assembly steps between retrieval and generation can each silently degrade or drop the correct chunk.

promptText: In a multi-agent system, what is the key tradeoff between giving sub-agents a shared context versus isolated context per agent?
options: Shared context keeps agents coordinated but means every agent's window grows with every other agent's output, so one agent's verbose or hallucinated content pollutes everyone else's context; isolated context keeps each agent focused and lets it use a smaller model, but requires an explicit handoff mechanism to pass curated results between agents
Shared context is strictly superior in every scenario because it eliminates the need for any handoff logic between agents
Isolated context is strictly superior in every scenario because it guarantees agents never produce inconsistent results
The choice between shared and isolated context has no effect on token cost or coordination quality
explanation: Most production multi-agent designs land on a hybrid: isolated working context per agent, plus a curated, deliberately small shared summary layer that a supervisor maintains and passes down, rather than choosing one extreme.

promptText: When selecting a subset of candidate context items (retrieved chunks, memory facts) under a fixed token budget, why should you rank by 'relevance per token' rather than by raw relevance score alone?
options: A highly relevant but extremely long chunk may cost the budget for three shorter, nearly-as-relevant chunks that collectively would have served the answer better -- this is a lightweight knapsack problem where cost (tokens) and value (relevance) must both be weighed, and a greedy value-per-cost heuristic approximates the optimum cheaply and deterministically
Raw relevance score is always a perfect predictor of answer quality, so no cost weighting is ever needed
Token cost should be ignored entirely because all retrieved chunks are truncated to the same fixed length before selection
Relevance-per-token ranking is mathematically identical to raw relevance ranking and produces the same selection in every case
explanation: Production systems rarely run exact knapsack optimization; a greedy value-per-cost heuristic is fast, deterministic, and debuggable, which matters more than squeezing out marginal theoretical optimality given that relevance scores are themselves estimates.
